pedagogy.summary: This topic delivers the key mechanical insight about muscles: a muscle can only PULL (it contracts, getting shorter and fatter) — it cannot push. Because of this, muscles must work in opposing PAIRS to move a bone both ways: at the elbow, the biceps contracts to BEND the arm while the triceps relaxes, and to STRAIGHTEN it the triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes. This 'one pulls, the other relaxes' antagonistic pair is the heart of the topic and directly explains why we have pairs of muscles at joints. The second idea is the voluntary/involuntary distinction: some muscles we consciously control (arm, leg — voluntary), while others work automatically without us thinking (the heart, and the muscles that push food through the digestive system — involuntary). Teach it on the child's own arm (feel the biceps bunch when you bend, feel it relax when you straighten) so the pair is felt directly. The must-fix misconception is 'muscles push things back' — they don't; the partner muscle pulls the other way.
bestPractices: Teach 'muscles PULL, never push' first, felt on the child's own upper arm (biceps bunches when bending), because everything else follows from it.
Demonstrate the antagonistic PAIR at the elbow: biceps contracts + triceps relaxes to bend; triceps contracts + biceps relaxes to straighten — the pair is why both directions are possible.
Have children feel BOTH muscles as they move (one hardens/shortens while the other softens), making 'contract' and 'relax' concrete opposites.
Introduce voluntary vs involuntary with clear examples (arm/leg = voluntary you control; heart and gut muscles = involuntary, automatic), linking back to circulation and digestion.
Use a simple hinge model (two elastic bands on either side of a cardboard joint) so the pull-only, work-in-pairs logic is visible and manipulable.
keyRepresentations: Elbow antagonistic-pair diagram: biceps and triceps, one contracting while the other relaxes
The child's own arm as the manipulative (feel biceps bunch/relax when bending and straightening)
'Muscles pull, can't push' shown by a muscle shortening to move a bone
A hinge-joint model with an elastic band on each side (pull one way, then the other)
Voluntary vs involuntary sort (arm/leg vs heart/gut) with 'do you choose to move it?'
commonMisconceptions: 'Muscles push bones back into place' — muscles only PULL; the opposing muscle pulls the bone the other way.
'A single muscle moves a bone both ways' — missing that opposing pairs are needed because muscles can't push.
'When a muscle relaxes it goes limp/does nothing important' — relaxing is an active part of the pair's teamwork, letting its partner pull.
'All muscles are under our control' — missing involuntary muscles (heart, digestive muscles) that work automatically.
'The heart is not a muscle' — it is an involuntary muscle that never rests.
'Bigger muscle = the one that straightens' or other guesses — rather than reasoning from which muscle is contracting.

learn.summary: Teach that skeletal muscles can only PULL (they contract, getting shorter and fatter) and never push. Because of this, muscles must work in opposing (antagonistic) pairs to move a bone both ways: at the elbow, the biceps contracts to bend the arm while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to straighten it while the biceps relaxes. This is felt best on the child's own upper arm. Second idea: some muscles are voluntary (arm, leg — we choose) and some are involuntary (heart, digestive muscles — automatic). The key misconception to fix is 'muscles push things back' — the partner muscle pulls the other way, and a relaxing muscle does nothing active.

activities.title: Feel the pair on your own arm
feedback: If the learner says one muscle pushes the arm straight again: muscles only pull — press your palm down on the table to straighten the arm, and feel that the biceps softens while the triceps on the other side tightens and pulls the arm straight.
If they think the relaxing muscle pushes the limb back: a relaxing muscle just softens and lets go; it is the OPPOSITE muscle contracting that moves the bone back.
Prompt: which side tightens when you bend? Which side tightens when you straighten? That is your pair.
activities.rationale: Using the child's own arm makes contract/relax and the pull-only property directly perceptible, grounding the mechanism in bodily experience before any diagram. The source supports the underlying fact being made perceptible (muscles produce movement only by pulling, in antagonistic pairs); it does not by itself establish that felt experience is the most effective medium.
sourceClaims: Skeletal muscles produce movement only by contracting (pulling), so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs (e.g. biceps and triceps) to move a bone in both directions; cardiac and smooth (e.g. digestive) muscle are involuntary.
learnerActions: Place your free hand on the front of your upper arm (the biceps), then bend your elbow to raise your forearm — notice the biceps bunch up, getting shorter and harder.

Keeping your hand there, straighten your arm by pressing your palm firmly down on a table top (or pushing against a wall) — feel the biceps soften. (If you just let your forearm lower slowly on its own, gravity does most of the work and the biceps stays partly tight to control the fall, so the change is harder to feel.)

Now feel the back of your upper arm (the triceps) and press down on the table again to straighten the arm: notice that the back (triceps) tightens while the front relaxes. Straightening against a push like this is what makes the triceps work hard enough to feel.
Say out loud each time: 'Which muscle is pulling now, and which has relaxed?'
activities.intendedInsight: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls a bone; it cannot push. To move the bone back the other way, a second muscle on the opposite side must contract and pull — this is the antagonistic pair. 'Contract' and 'relax' are concrete opposites you can feel.

activities.title: Drive the elbow and discover why a pair is needed
feedback: If the learner expects one muscle to do both jobs: try moving the bone back with only that muscle — it can haul the bone one way but cannot push it back, so you need its partner.
Confirm correct reasoning: yes — the biceps pulls the arm up (bend), the triceps pulls it down (straighten); while one pulls, the other relaxes.
Challenge question: if BOTH muscles pulled hard at the same time, what would happen to the arm? (The opposing pulls roughly cancel, so the arm is held stiff and does not swing either way.)
activities.rationale: Letting the learner drive the joint and fail to push the bone back with a single side turns 'why a pair is needed' into an experienced result rather than a told fact. An elastic-band-on-each-side hinge or a live rig makes the pull-only logic visible and manipulable; this is a proposed scaffold, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Skeletal muscles produce movement only by contracting (pulling), so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs (e.g. biceps and triceps) to move a bone in both directions; cardiac and smooth (e.g. digestive) muscle are involuntary.
learnerActions: Use a model of the elbow (a driveable on-screen rig, or a cardboard hinge with an elastic band fixed on each side) where each side can act like a muscle pulling.
Make the biceps side pull only (on the band model, pull/tighten the biceps-side band to mimic the muscle contracting — shortening and pulling): watch the forearm swing up as it pulls — the arm bends.
Now try to use that SAME side to push the arm back down straight. Observe that it can only pull one way; it cannot push the bone back.
Make the triceps side pull (the other band): the arm straightens because this muscle now pulls the other way.
State the rule: one muscle pulls to bend, the other pulls to straighten, because neither can push.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a muscle can only ever pull, a single muscle can move a bone one way but is powerless to return it — so a second, opposing muscle is required. This is why muscles come in antagonistic pairs at a joint.

activities.title: Voluntary or involuntary? Sort the muscles
feedback: If the learner claims all muscles are voluntary / that you could stop your heart by deciding to: you can choose to bend your arm, but your heart keeps beating whether you think about it or not — it is involuntary.
If they think the heart is not a muscle: the heart is a muscle, but an involuntary one that works automatically all the time.
Link back: the muscles that move food through digestion also work by themselves, without you choosing.
activities.rationale: An explicit contrast with a clear decision test ('can you choose to stop it?') separates voluntary from involuntary and anchors it to the examples the curriculum names, connecting to circulation and digestion. A sort can teach and check this classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or an explanation.
sourceClaims: Skeletal muscles produce movement only by contracting (pulling), so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs (e.g. biceps and triceps) to move a bone in both directions; cardiac and smooth (e.g. digestive) muscle are involuntary.
learnerActions: For each muscle, ask: 'Do I choose to move it, or does it work on its own?'
Sort examples: arm muscles and leg muscles (voluntary — you decide), the heart and the muscles that squeeze food along the digestive system (involuntary — automatic).
Try the test: you can decide to bend your arm — but try to decide to stop your heart from beating. You cannot. That shows it is involuntary.
Name at least one involuntary muscle from memory (heart; digestive/gut muscles) and explain why automatic control is useful (it keeps you alive without you having to think about it).
activities.intendedInsight: Voluntary muscles are under conscious control; involuntary muscles (the heart, digestive muscles) work automatically without any decision. The heart IS a muscle — an involuntary one that never stops working, all your life.

activities.title: Consolidation check
feedback: For contract/relax questions, reason from which muscle is pulling for that movement — do not guess by size (the bigger muscle is not automatically the straightener).
If an answer attributes the return movement to a muscle pushing, re-state: muscles only pull; the partner pulls the other way.
Reward transfer: correctly applying 'pairs because muscles only pull' to a new joint shows real understanding.
activities.rationale: A short recall/categorisation task consolidates the core after the hands-on work. It checks and reinforces classification and recall, but a sort or match does not itself elicit the discovery that a single muscle cannot push the bone back — the driving/feeling activities provide that.
learnerActions: For a given movement (e.g. bending the arm), say which muscle contracts and which relaxes.
Categorise a list of muscles as voluntary or involuntary.
Match each action (bend arm / straighten arm) to the muscle that pulls to produce it.
Transfer: explain how a pair would work at another joint, or name another involuntary muscle.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates that muscles pull in opposing pairs and that voluntary and involuntary muscles differ, including applying the reasoning to a new joint or muscle.

constraints: Learners aged roughly 7–9; conceptual topic within 'Animals including humans'.

The decisive teaching goal is the DYNAMIC, felt mechanism: contract/relax and pull-only driving why pairs are needed. A static labelled biceps/triceps picture can show the pair's layout but does not let the learner experience contract-while-partner-relaxes; use it only as a reference scaffold alongside the felt/manipulable work.

A recognition/categorisation check (which muscle contracts, voluntary vs involuntary sorting) consolidates and assesses classification but does not itself elicit the discovery that a single muscle cannot push the bone back — keep the driving/feeling activities for that.

A hinge-with-elastic-bands model or an on-screen rig is an approximation of a real elbow: label it as a model, and note the real joint and muscles are more complex than two bands; an elastic band is pulled/stretched to mimic a muscle contracting.

The textbook biceps/triceps antagonistic model is a KS2 simplification; in everyday straightening of a hanging forearm gravity assists, so treat 'triceps contracts to straighten' as the taught model rather than a claim about every real movement.

Must-fix misconceptions to confront, not reinforce: 'muscles push bones back', 'one muscle moves a bone both ways', 'a relaxing muscle actively pushes', 'all muscles are voluntary', and 'the heart is not a muscle'.
Keep examples of involuntary muscles curriculum-accurate: the heart and the digestive-system muscles.
An optional 3D arm may add rotational realism but no conceptual gain for this planar hinge; it is an optional alternative, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted the dynamic result is 'impossible on a static image and unnecessary in 3D' and that a 3D arm 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-format preferences, not established pedagogical laws; softened to scoped claims (a fixed picture cannot be manipulated; a driveable model lets learners experience contract/relax) and the 3D option retained only as optional realism.

The Britannica claim (antagonistic pairs; cardiac/smooth muscle involuntary) is marked verified:false in the row; the National Curriculum claim is verified:true. Comparative efficacy of interactive vs static vs 3D media is not established by these sources, so efficacy wording is kept as proposed/may/intended.

The row described the heart as a muscle that 'never rests'; corrected in the guidance to 'never stops working', since cardiac muscle relaxes between beats but keeps working throughout life. The original inaccuracy is recorded here, not offered to learners.

Self-audit: the 'both muscles pull at once' probe is handled as a reasoning question (opposing pulls roughly cancel; arm held stiff) rather than asserted as a fixed fact, since detailed co-contraction exceeds this age band.
Self-audit: avoided the 'bigger muscle straightens' guessing pattern by instructing learners to reason from which muscle is contracting.

Self-audit: the mechanism source claim is attached to the felt/driving/sorting activities because it supports the factual principle being taught; it does not evidence that any particular medium is more effective, which remains untested.

probeDeeper: Feel your upper arm as you bend and then straighten it — which side tightens each time?
Name another muscle that works automatically without you deciding — think about what happens to food after you swallow.
If BOTH muscles in the pair pulled hard at the same time, what would happen to your arm?
assess.correctAnswer: Because muscles only pull, they work in opposing PAIRS: the biceps contracts (pulls) to bend the arm while the triceps relaxes; to straighten it, the triceps contracts (pulls) the other way while the biceps relaxes. One muscle can't push the arm back, so a second muscle pulls it the other way. You can choose to bend your arm because the arm muscles are voluntary; the heart is an involuntary muscle that works automatically, so you can't decide to stop it — which keeps you alive without having to think about it.

errorPatterns.pattern: A single muscle pushes the bone back to straighten the arm (muscles push as well as pull).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reaffirm muscles only pull; introduce the triceps as the partner that pulls the arm straight — an antagonistic pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: The same muscle pushes the arm back out to straighten it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the biceps pushes the arm straight again.

errorPatterns.pattern: When a muscle relaxes it actively pushes the limb the other way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify that a relaxing muscle does nothing active; the OPPOSITE muscle contracting is what moves the bone back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the return movement to the relaxing muscle pushing.

errorPatterns.pattern: All muscles are voluntary — you could control your heart if you tried.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate voluntary (you choose) from involuntary (automatic); heart and gut muscles run without your decision.
errorPatterns.distractor: You could stop your heart just by deciding to, like bending your arm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims the heartbeat is under conscious control.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks one muscle both bends and straightens by pushing and pulling, or thinks the heart is under conscious control.
responseLevels.full: Explains the antagonistic pair (one pulls to bend, the other pulls to straighten, because muscles only pull) AND distinguishes voluntary from involuntary muscles with correct examples — transferring to another joint or involuntary muscle.
responseLevels.partial: Knows muscles work in pairs OR distinguishes voluntary/involuntary, but not both, or can't explain WHY a pair is needed (that muscles only pull).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A muscle can only PULL, never push. So how can your arm both bend AND straighten again, if the muscle that bent it can't push it back out? And why can you decide to bend your arm, but you can't decide to stop your heart from beating?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks one muscle pushes the arm back, or that the heart is under conscious control, misses the core ideas. Only a child who grasps 'muscles only pull, so you need a pair' AND voluntary/involuntary answers both. The tier-two heart question forces the involuntary idea, which a pairs-only answer wouldn't reveal.
